Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: The threat items are oriented toward external environmental danger (scanning surroundings, planning escape routes), which is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 68-year-old policy analyst unless there is an additional trauma context not represented here.

Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance reinforces an expectation of unpredictable external danger, which fits assault/combat-type trauma more than illness trauma and does not cohere well with the rest of the illness-based profile.

Memory: Guilt on Recall and Negative Appraisals: Character Blame imply a strong self-blame/guilt formulation, but the other selected items center on current danger vigilance and emotional loss; for life-threatening illness, this specific self-blame pattern is possible but, combined with the external-danger threat items, creates a clinically incoherent mix of trauma themes.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, persistent escape-route scanning is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. It implies imminent external attack or entrapment rather than illness-related threat, while the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger and emotional change.

Intense guilt on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals focus on permanent emotional loss and bodily alarm rather than responsibility for causing harm or failing others. The guilt theme lacks support elsewhere in memory or appraisals.

'The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am' suggests a strong characterological self-blame formulation. In a life-threatening illness case, that can occur, but in this profile it is not well integrated with the other selected appraisals, which focus on bodily danger and emotional numbing. Together with guilt on recall, it introduces a self-blame theme that is otherwise unsupported.

vignette:
Samuel, a 68-year-old African American man, sat in the therapist's office, his hands clasped tightly together. He was a policy analyst who had spent decades shaping public policy, yet in this moment, he felt utterly out of control. The room was quiet, but the tension in his body spoke volumes. He had come to realize that his life had taken an unexpected turn after he was diagnosed with a life-threatening illness two years prior. The memory of that diagnosis still loomed large in his mind, and as he sat there, he could feel the sensation of dread creeping back in.

The day he received the news was etched in his memory with stark clarity. He had gone in for what he thought was a routine check-up, only to be met with his doctor’s grave expression. “You have cancer,” the doctor had said, and those words sent his world spiraling. Samuel remembered how the walls of the small examination room began to close in around him, as if the very air had thickened. He could recall the way his heart raced and how his hands trembled, but then, as the doctor continued talking about treatment options, he felt a strange numbness wash over him. It was as though he were watching a scene unfold from a distance, a spectator in his own life.

Months passed, and Samuel found himself grappling with an overwhelming sense of alertness. Even within the familiar confines of his home, where he had always felt safe, he could not shake the feeling that danger lurked just around the corner. The once-comforting sound of his creaking floorboards now sent his heart racing. He would jump at the slightest noise, his body tensed and ready to react, as if he were still in that examination room faced with the specter of his illness. The very space that had once felt like a sanctuary now felt like a battleground. Samuel had come to believe that his body was his enemy, an unreliable vessel that betrayed him with every pang of anxiety.

As days turned into weeks, he noticed his concentration slipping. The reports he used to analyze with ease now felt like insurmountable obstacles. He would sit at his desk, staring blankly at the screen, frustration mounting as he struggled to process information. This inability to focus gnawed at him, amplifying his fears that he would never regain control over his own mind. Each time he attempted to recall the details of his diagnosis or treatment, he would be hit by a wave of grief and despair so overwhelming that he would have to stop working altogether. It was as if those memories were too heavy to carry, echoing through his mind with a clarity that felt like a fresh trauma.

Samuel had lost his wife a few years before his diagnosis, and the emotional scars ran deep. He often found himself reflecting on the life they had shared, the laughter, the warmth, the ordinary moments that now felt impossibly distant. He had come to believe that he would never again feel the range of human emotions he once took for granted. The notion of feeling “normal” seemed like a distant dream, locked away in a past that felt irretrievably lost. Samuel felt as though he were a stranger in his own skin, disconnected from the vibrant life he used to lead.

His relationships with family and friends began to fray under the weight of his internal struggles. Social gatherings became insurmountable challenges. He would often find excuses to avoid them, fearing that the energy required to engage would expose him to feelings he was not ready to confront. The isolation crept in slowly, but now, it felt like a suffocating blanket, wrapping him tighter with each passing day. He feared being judged for his emotions, or worse, being seen as weak.

It was this growing sense of isolation that finally propelled Samuel to seek help. He had come to realize that he could no longer navigate this tumultuous sea alone. The thought of sharing his fears and feelings with a therapist stirred a mix of hope and apprehension within him. He feared that he might be judged or that he would be unable to articulate the depth of his pain. Yet, the prospect of feeling even a glimmer of connection or understanding drove him forward. Samuel longed to reclaim a sense of normalcy, to break free from the prison his mind had constructed. Perhaps, with help, he could begin to trust his body and emotions again, and slowly rediscover the man he once was.
